newsitem.title: USA: Natural gas prices soar, oil falls.
newsitem.headline: Natural gas prices soar, oil falls.

text.p: Natural gas prices jumped Wednesday after data showed inventories rose less than had been expected, but oil prices ended lower amid worries that a three-month long rally was faltering.

On the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), natural gas futures for November delivery rose more than five cents to more than $2.50 for 1,000 cubic feet after the American Gas Association data showed stocks rose only 38 billion cubic feet to 82 percent of capacity in the latest week.
That fell well below traders' expectations that stocks would rise by about twice that level.
Meanwhile, NYMEX November crude futures matched last April's post-Gulf War high at $25.70 a barrel then slumped $1.00 before recovering to settle down 25 cents at $25.17.

Heating oil futures were even more volatile, with November first rising almost 1.5 cents to 74.40 cents a gallon after weekly data from the American Petroleum Institute showed heating oil stocks dropped again last week in the key northeast region, leaving them some 18 million barrels below last year's levels at 24 million barrels.
But traders were spooked that the bull run, having pushed heating oil up 50 percent in the last three-and-a-half months, may be faltering.

The declining stocks behind the rise has led to calls for political action to ensure vulnerable consumers aren't hit. Though the Energy Department is on record saying it will not intervene in the market, there has been persistant speculation among market participants that companies may agree to take voluntary action.
A meeting this Friday between oil company executives and Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary to discuss the problem contributed to the market's jumpiness.
"There is a sense within the industry that they better do something and that's enough to make people rather cautious," said Steve Platt, an energy analyst at brokerage Dean Witter.
Weakness in oil prices led to a fall in the Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 commodities of 1.83 points to 244.41 on Wednesday.

Lumber prices on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange rose their daily trading limit on the key November contract, boosted partly by talk that Canadian mills may have met their yearly export quota to the U.S. ahead of time.
"Increased rumours, relative to the quota, continued to lead to speculative buying" in futures, said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney Forest Products analyst.
Under an agreement between Ottawa and Washington, export fees will be imposed on Canadian lumber exports exceeding 14.7 billion feet a year. The agreement became effective on April 1.
The talk led to concern that shipments from Canada may slow down during the next few months.
November lumber closed up $10 for 1,000 board feet at $398.70 at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
Soybeans on the Chicago Board of Trade closed lower, depressed partly by talk that the late planted U.S. crop may be yielding at a higher level than many had anticipated.

"We're seeing yields mostly in the mid-40s to mid-50s (bushels per acre)," said Fred Gent, grain manager at McLean County Service Co in Bloomington, Ill. "I don't think we expected quite that good but that's about average for us."
The Department of Agriculture reported this week the soybean harvest was 40 percent complete as of Sunday.
"Rain in the forecast firmed the market early but it couldn't hold. The market just cannot hold rallies," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
November soybeans fell two cents to $6.91 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
